node.description: Canadian historian who connected military institutions and soldiers’ experience with social and labour history. John Bullen reads Working People as a synthesis linking labour disputes and political organization, while Morton’s own2018 recollections interpret war remembrance through national formation. These placements describe different strands of his writing; coauthors Terry Copp and Glenn T. Wright retain their credit.

named_group_routes.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

named_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

named_group_routes.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1). It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.

named_group_routes.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

named_group_routes.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.

named_group_routes.relationship: Limited identities and regional explanation criticised from a class standpoint: 'limited identities' as 'neither "limited" nor analytically separable' (1978), region as 'the crucial variable' 'increasingly misplaced' and western exceptionalism overstated (1981), and the 1919 revolt as 'national in character' (1984)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, in period. Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: Cook and Careless 'called for a turn away from nation and politics' toward 'region, ethnicity and class' (p. 116, citing Cook 1967 and Careless 1969); 'The call for attention to "limited identities" was the death-knell of Laurentianism' (p. 117); 'The long-overdue insertion of a class analysis into Canadian historical writing already promises overviews which transcend the refreshing and liberating pluralism of the 1960s calls for attention to region, ethnicity and class. It should be increasingly clear, however, that these so-called "limited identities" are neither "limited" nor analytically separable. No historical notion of class (and there can be no other useful notion) can fail to incorporate ethnicity and place' (p. 135). Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), read in full: 'NONE CAN DENY the importance of regional differences … Yet the increasing emphasis placed on "region" as the crucial variable which explains sundry problems of Canadian development seems increasingly misplaced', citing Westfall on the regional interpretation standing 'the old nationalist history on its head' (p. 74); before the 1890s 'there was not one Canadian working class but many' (p. 75); accounts of western workers are shaped by 'a strong sense of western exceptionalism', and 'the rather easy assumptions of a unique western working-class militancy have been overstated', with n. 25: 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this' (p. 76); 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere … This celebration of region has fit very well with the general direction of Canadian political life in the last decade. Surely the time has come to begin to reflect on region in a critical way' (p. 76); his remedy is not 'A return to an old national history? No, of course not, but rather the consideration on a national scale of the particular class experiences of Canadian workers in local and regional contexts which adds up to something more than local and regional exceptionalism' (p. 77). '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt', Labour/Le Travail 13 (1984), pp. 11–44, read at pp. 11–17: 'These examples are intended simply to demonstrate that the revolt was national in character and that its seeds were not rooted in any unique regional fermentation. The "radical" west and the conservative east have become sorry shibboleths of Canadian historiography'; 'the similarities of struggle begin to outweigh the initial impression of regional particularism' (p. 15). Qualifications kept: he grants 'the importance of regional differences' (1981, p. 74) and calls Maritime underdevelopment real (pp. 75–76); the 1978 sentence welcomes the 1960s pluralism as 'refreshing and liberating' before arguing that class analysis transcends it. In-period reading: Morton (2000, p. 25, read) credits Kealey, Palmer, Heron, Hann and others with bringing labour history 'back from superstructure, politics, and the exceptionalism of Western Canada to regions that had been largely neglected by their predecessors: Ontario and the Maritimes'. No reply by Bercuson to the 1981 or 1984 regional argument was checked. Distinct from Cook's 1977–83 critique of regionalism (edge from ramsay_cook to cdn_regional), which doubts region as a unit; Kealey's subordinates it to class and national-scale capitalism.

named_group_routes.relationship: Herbert Gutman's cultural history of American workers and David Montgomery's workers' control as models for Kealey's Toronto studies (1976–81), as Kealey and his reviewers said, with the criticisms of Gutman he reported and Brody's verdict that he did not follow Gutman's method
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statements. 1976 (Labour/Le Travailleur 1, read at pp. 32–34, 58): 'David Montgomery has suggested that we must look beyond pre-industrial cultural forms if we are to understand the behaviour of skilled workers', who were 'veterans of industrial life' (p. 33); on the meaning of shop-floor power, 'David Montgomery has argued that the major impact of this early workers' control was the skilled workers' growing awareness that the key institution for the transformation of society was the trade union' (p. 58). 1978 (Acadiensis, p. 117): the works of Thompson and Hobsbawm, 'and later of Americans such as Herbert Gutman and David Montgomery, had their effects in Canada on a new generation of graduate students'. 1981 (Labour/Le Travailleur 7, read in full): 'A cultural approach in American work on labour history also generated a significant breakthrough. Most notably associated with Herbert Gutman' (p. 81); n. 33: 'Gutman's influence can be seen in numerous recent studies. In Canada see Palmer, A Culture in Conflict and Kealey, Toronto Workers' (p. 82). He reports Dubofsky's and Montgomery's worry about 'the failure to consider the political and economic context' and Brody's charge that Gutman 'shifted the Thompsonian focus on class and culture into a focus solely on culture' (pp. 81–82). In-period readers. David Brody (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, read): 'During his tenure at Rochester a decade or so ago, Herbert G. Gutman built up a remarkable graduate program in American working-class history … Gregory Kealey's book bears the marks of what might be termed the Gutman school' (p. 361); but 'In one crucial way, unfortunately, it does not': Gutman 'invariably has drawn his ideas out from the evidence', and 'Had he adhered to the prudent craft of his mentor, Kealey might have written a powerful book' (p. 364). Morton (2000, pp. 22–23, read): the 'second generation' 'travelled abroad, to Warwick, Rochester, and Binghamton, to meet their American and British mentors', and the Knights of Labor records 'Kealey had been able to study at Rochester'. Later engagement, title level only: 'Herbert G. Gutman, 1928–1985, and the Writing of Working-Class History' (Monthly Review, 1986) and 'Gutman and Montgomery' (ILWCH, 1990; wcreq_kealey_1990). Gutman and Montgomery are historians on the newleft roster (work_cultures strand). Influence, not discipleship: the 1981 essay also gives Thompson and Williams as touchstones, and edge_890 carries Thompson's place in the field. edge_888 (newleft ↔ cdn_working_class) stays as the group-level comparison.

named_group_routes.relationship: Co-authors of Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and allies in the new labour history, read together by critics as 'the Kealey-Palmer claims', though 'differently positioned politically' (Sangster) and with different emphases: workers' control and class analysis for Kealey, craft culture for Palmer
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Collaboration, in their own texts. Kealey's 1976 essay thanks Palmer, with David Frank and Craig Heron, for comments (p. 32 n.); the 1981 essay thanks him among others (p. 94), refers readers to Palmer's forthcoming Making of E.P. Thompson (p. 82), and says that 'Kealey and Palmer, "Dreaming of What Might Be"' 'argues this position at length' on the value of the romantic and utopian traditions, which gave workers 'the ability to dream of an alternative future' (p. 84 and n. 39). Read together by critics, in period. Bercuson (1981, p. 96): 'the Palmer and Kealey books' as 'restricted but intensive studies'. Bradbury (Labour/Le Travail 19, 1987, pp. 35–36, read) quotes Dreaming (p. 318) and writes that to dismiss partially a Knights of Labor editor's picture of a wife who 'can darn a stocking' 'as "offensive" and as "crude moralizing," as Kealey and Palmer do, seems to me both to deny the realities of the division of labour within the working-class family economy at that time, and to close off the possibility of examining this very important element of a skilled worker's pride'; she adds that 'Kealey and Palmer quite rightly point out' that a Montreal workman's statement stopped short of a critique of 'women's proper sphere'. Sangster (Labour/Le Travail 46, 2000, p. 133, read): 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere.' Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; Stanley Ryerson (1981, as Morton reports it) argued that the Knights were 'devoutly committed to labour-employer harmony and industrial peace'. Later reading, labelled: McCoy (2021) quotes their chapter: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). The book itself is unread. A comparison, not an influence: the edge records co-authorship and joint reception. Their different emphases are recorded in edge_919 (Palmer's craft culture) and pe138_kealey_rel_01 (Kealey's workers' control and class analysis).
